title: Martyrdom and the dead
def: The Quran says that those killed in God’s way are alive with their Lord (3:169).
what: “Do not think of those who are killed in God’s way as dead; they are alive with their Lord, provided for” (3:169; also 2:154). A shahīd is a witness, and in practice a person killed defending the faith, or in defence of life and property, as the Prophet said (Sahih al-Bukhari). Those who die of plague, drowning or childbirth are also counted as such in hadith.
misread: That Islam rewards killing oneself and others.
sources: The Quran says “do not kill yourselves” (4:29), and the Prophet said that whoever kills himself will be punished by the same means in the Fire (Sahih al-Bukhari). Muslim scholars have broadly condemned suicide attacks on civilians, and the Prophet forbade killing of non-combatants.

title: Maryam
def: Mary, mother of Jesus: the only woman named in the Quran, which gives her a chapter.
what: The Quran says that the angels told her God had chosen and purified her above the women of the worlds (3:42). Chapter 19 is named after her, and chapter 66 holds her up as a model of faith and chastity (66:12). The Prophet is reported to have said that the best of women were Mary, daughter of Imran, and Khadija (Sahih al-Bukhari).
misread: That the Quran confuses Mary with Miriam, Aaron’s sister, because it calls her “sister of Aaron” (19:28).
sources: A man once raised this with the Prophet’s Companion al-Mughira ibn Shu’ba, who asked the Prophet and was told that the people of that time used to take names from the prophets and righteous people who came before them (Sahih Muslim). “Sister of Aaron” can mean one of his line or his kind, as the Arabic akh and ukht often do. The Quran also gives her father’s name as Imran, as the Bible gives Amram for Aaron’s father.

title: Modesty and dress
def: The Quran asks both men and women to guard their gaze and chastity and to dress modestly.
what: “Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts… and tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts and not display their adornment except what is apparent” (24:30–31). Among the signs of success are those who guard their chastity (23:5, 70:29). “The garment of piety, that is best” (7:26). The Prophet said that modesty is part of faith (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: The commands are given to both sexes, and are read by scholars differently on what counts as “apparent”. The Quran also tells believers to dress well for prayer: “take your adornment at every place of prayer” (7:31).

title: Mothers and childbirth
def: The Quran honours mothers for the hardship of carrying and bearing children.
what: “We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents; his mother bore him in hardship and gave birth to him in hardship” (46:15; also 31:14). Mary’s labour pains are told in 19:23. The Prophet, asked who most deserved good company, said “your mother”, three times, before “your father” (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Mushaf
def: A written copy of the Quran bound between two covers.
what: From ṣaḥīfa, “a leaf”. In the Prophet’s lifetime the Quran was written on whatever was at hand and memorised in full by many. After his death the leaves were collected, and in the time of Uthman copies in one agreed spelling were sent to the main centres. The standard copy is often called the Uthmanic mushaf.
A mushaf is handled with respect, and Muslims traditionally wash before touching it.
misread: That Uthman “burned the rival Qurans”, destroying the true text.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari records that Uthman had the leaves copied, ordered the standard copies sent out, and asked that other individual leaves be destroyed to avoid disputes. Muslims read this as protecting one text for the whole community, and note that no major dispute over it was recorded in the early centuries.

title: Music and singing
def: Muslim scholars have differed about music: some forbid instruments, many allow singing and the frame drum, and Muslim civilisations have produced much music.
what: Reports show the Prophet allowing singing and drumming at weddings and at the feast of Eid, for example when Aisha’s household had girls singing and he told Abu Bakr to leave them (Sahih al-Bukhari). A woman who had vowed to play the daf if he returned safely was told to fulfil her vow (Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi). A report in Sahih al-Bukhari that speaks of people who will permit “musical instruments” is discussed by scholars for its wording.
sources: Al-Ghazali allowed music as long as it did not lead to sin, and Ibn Hazm denied that any sound hadith forbids it. Others, such as many Hanbalis and Salafis, forbid stringed instruments. Muslim societies have a long musical tradition, including Quranic recitation (tajwīd), the call to prayer, Sufi chant and classical music.
